sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: Chapter I.

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: The beginning of things.

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: They were not railway children to begin with.

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: I don't suppose they had ever thought about railways except as a means of getting to Maskelyne and Cook's, the Pantomime, Zoological Gardens, and Madame Tussaud's.

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: They were just ordinary suburban children, and they lived with their Father and Mother in an ordinary red-brick-fronted villa, with coloured glass in the front door, a tiled passage that was called a hall, a bath-room with hot and cold water, electric bells, French windows, and a good deal of white paint, and 'every modern convenience', as the house-agents say.

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: There were three of them.

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: Roberta was the eldest. Of course, Mothers never have favourites, but if their Mother HAD had a favourite, it might have been Roberta.

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: Next came Peter, who wished to be an Engineer when he grew up; and the youngest was Phyllis, who meant extremely well.

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: Mother did not spend all her time in paying dull calls to dull ladies, and sitting dully at home waiting for dull ladies to pay calls to her.

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: She was almost always there, ready to play with the children, and read to them, and help them to do their home-lessons.

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: Besides this she used to write stories for them while they were at school, and read them aloud after tea, and she always made up funny pieces of poetry for their birthdays and for other great occasions, such as the christening of the new kittens, or the refurnishing of the doll's house, or the time when they were getting over the mumps.

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: These three lucky children always had everything they needed: pretty clothes, good fires, a lovely nursery with heaps of toys, and a Mother Goose wall-paper.

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: They had a kind and merry nursemaid, and a dog who was called James, and who was their very own.

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: They also had a Father who was just perfect--never cross, never unjust, and always ready for a game--at least, if at any time he was NOT ready, he always had an excellent reason for it, and explained the reason to the children so interestingly and funnily that they felt sure he couldn't help himself.

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: You will think that they ought to have been very happy.

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: And so they were, but they did not know HOW happy till the pretty life in the Red Villa was over and done with, and they had to live a very different life indeed.

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: The dreadful change came quite suddenly.

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: Peter had a birthday--his tenth.

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: Among his other presents was a model engine more perfect than you could ever have dreamed of.

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: The other presents were full of charm, but the Engine was fuller of charm than any of the others were.

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: Its charm lasted in its full perfection for exactly three days.

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: Then, owing either to Peter's inexperience or Phyllis's good intentions, which had been rather pressing, or to some other cause, the Engine suddenly went off with a bang.

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: James was so frightened that he went out and did not come back all day.

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: All the Noah's Ark people who were in the tender were broken to bits, but nothing else was hurt except the poor little engine and the feelings of Peter.

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: The others said he cried over it--but of course boys of ten do not cry, however terrible the tragedies may be which darken their lot.

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: He said that his eyes were red because he had a cold.

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: This turned out to be true, though Peter did not know it was when he said it, the next day he had to go to bed and stay there.

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: Mother began to be afraid that he might be sickening for measles, when suddenly he sat up in bed and said:

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: “I hate gruel--I hate barley water--I hate bread and milk.

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: I want to get up and have something REAL to eat.”

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: “What would you like?

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: Mother asked.

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: “A pigeon-pie,” said Peter, eagerly, “a large pigeon-pie.

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: A very large one.”

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: So Mother asked the Cook to make a large pigeon-pie.

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: The pie was made.

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: And when the pie was made, it was cooked.

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: And when it was cooked, Peter ate some of it.

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: After that his cold was better.

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: Mother made a piece of poetry to amuse him while the pie was being made.

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: It began by saying what an unfortunate but worthy boy Peter was, then it went on:

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: He had an engine that he loved With all his heart and soul, And if he had a wish on earth It was to keep it whole.

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: One day--my friends, prepare your minds; I'm coming to the worst-- Quite suddenly a screw went mad, And then the boiler burst!

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: With gloomy face he picked it up And took it to his Mother, Though even he could not suppose That she could make another;

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: For those who perished on the line He did not seem to care, His engine being more to him Than all the people there.

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: And now you see the reason why Our Peter has been ill: He soothes his soul with pigeon-pie His gnawing grief to kill.

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: He wraps himself in blankets warm And sleeps in bed till late, Determined thus to overcome His miserable fate.

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: And if his eyes are rather red, His cold must just excuse it: Offer him pie; you may be sure He never will refuse it.

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: Father had been away in the country for three or four days.

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: All Peter's hopes for the curing of his afflicted Engine were now fixed on his Father, for Father was most wonderfully clever with his fingers.

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: He could mend all sorts of things.

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: He had often acted as veterinary surgeon to the wooden rocking-horse; once he had saved its life when all human aid was despaired of, and the poor creature was given up for lost, and even the carpenter said he didn't see his way to do anything.

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: And it was Father who mended the doll's cradle when no one else could; and with a little glue and some bits of wood and a pen-knife made all the Noah's Ark beasts as strong on their pins as ever they were, if not stronger.

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: Peter, with heroic unselfishness, did not say anything about his Engine till after Father had had his dinner and his after-dinner cigar.

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: The unselfishness was Mother's idea--but it was Peter who carried it out.

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: And needed a good deal of patience, too.

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: At last Mother said to Father, “Now, dear, if you're quite rested, and quite comfy, we want to tell you about the great railway accident, and ask your advice.”

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: “All right,” said Father, “fire away!”

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: So then Peter told the sad tale, and fetched what was left of the Engine.

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: “Hum,” said Father, when he had looked the Engine over very carefully.

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: The children held their breaths.

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: “Is there NO hope?” said Peter, in a low, unsteady voice.

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: “Hope?

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: Rather!

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: Tons of it,” said Father, cheerfully; “but it'll want something besides hope--a bit of brazing say, or some solder, and a new valve.

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: I think we'd better keep it for a rainy day.

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: In other words, I'll give up Saturday afternoon to it, and you shall all help me.”

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: “CAN girls help to mend engines?

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: Peter asked doubtfully.

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: “Of course they can.

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: Girls are just as clever as boys, and don't you forget it!

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: How would you like to be an engine-driver, Phil?”

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: “My face would be always dirty, wouldn't it?” said Phyllis, in unenthusiastic tones, “and I expect I should break something.”

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: “I should just love it,” said Roberta--“do you think I could when I'm grown up, Daddy?

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: Or even a stoker?”

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: “You mean a fireman,” said Daddy, pulling and twisting at the engine. “Well, if you still wish it, when you're grown up, we'll see about making you a fire-woman.

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: I remember when I was a boy--”

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: Just then there was a knock at the front door.

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: “Who on earth!” said Father. “An Englishman's house is his castle, of course, but I do wish they built semi-detached villas with moats and drawbridges.”

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: Ruth--she was the parlour-maid and had red hair--came in and said that two gentlemen wanted to see the master.

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: “I've shown them into the Library, Sir,” said she.

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: “I expect it's the subscription to the Vicar's testimonial,” said Mother, “or else it's the choir holiday fund.

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: Get rid of them quickly, dear.

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: It does break up an evening so, and it's nearly the children's bedtime.”

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: But Father did not seem to be able to get rid of the gentlemen at all quickly.

roomBlocks.text: to be able to get rid of the gentlemen at all quickly

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: “I wish we HAD got a moat and drawbridge,” said Roberta; “then, when we didn't want people, we could just pull up the drawbridge and no one else could get in.

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: I expect Father will have forgotten about when he was a boy if they stay much longer.”

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: Mother tried to make the time pass by telling them a new fairy story about a Princess with green eyes, but it was difficult because they could hear the voices of Father and the gentlemen in the Library, and Father's voice sounded louder and different to the voice he generally used to people who came about testimonials and holiday funds.

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: Then the Library bell rang, and everyone heaved a breath of relief.

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: “They're going now,” said Phyllis; “he's rung to have them shown out.”

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: But instead of showing anybody out, Ruth showed herself in, and she looked queer, the children thought.

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: “Please'm,” she said, “the Master wants you to just step into the study.

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: He looks like the dead, mum; I think he's had bad news.

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: You'd best prepare yourself for the worst, 'm--p'raps it's a death in the family or a bank busted or--”

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: “That'll do, Ruth,” said Mother gently; “you can go.”

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: Then Mother went into the Library.

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: There was more talking.

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: Then the bell rang again, and Ruth fetched a cab.

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: The children heard boots go out and down the steps.

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: The cab drove away, and the front door shut.

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: Then Mother came in.

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: Her dear face was as white as her lace collar, and her eyes looked very big and shining.

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: Her mouth looked like just a line of pale red--her lips were thin and not their proper shape at all.

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: “It's bedtime,” she said. “Ruth will put you to bed.”

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: “But you promised we should sit up late tonight because Father's come home,” said Phyllis.

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: “Father's been called away--on business,” said Mother. “Come, darlings, go at once.”

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: They kissed her and went.

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: Roberta lingered to give Mother an extra hug and to whisper:

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: “It wasn't bad news, Mammy, was it?

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: Is anyone dead--or--”

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: “Nobody's dead--no,” said Mother, and she almost seemed to push Roberta away. “I can't tell you anything tonight, my pet.

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: Go, dear, go NOW.”

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: So Roberta went.

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: Ruth brushed the girls' hair and helped them to undress. (Mother almost always did this herself.

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: When she had turned down the gas and left them she found Peter, still dressed, waiting on the stairs.

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: “I say, Ruth, what's up?” he asked.

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: “Don't ask me no questions and I won't tell you no lies,” the red-headed Ruth replied. “You'll know soon enough.”

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: Late that night Mother came up and kissed all three children as they lay asleep.

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: But Roberta was the only one whom the kiss woke, and she lay mousey-still, and said nothing.

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: “If Mother doesn't want us to know she's been crying,” she said to herself as she heard through the dark the catching of her Mother's breath, “we WON'T know it.

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: That's all.”

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: When they came down to breakfast the next morning, Mother had already gone out.

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: “To London,” Ruth said, and left them to their breakfast.

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: “There's something awful the matter,” said Peter, breaking his egg. “Ruth told me last night we should know soon enough.”

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: “Did you ASK her?” said Roberta, with scorn.

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: “Yes, I did!” said Peter, angrily. “If you could go to bed without caring whether Mother was worried or not, I couldn't.

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: So there.”

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: “I don't think we ought to ask the servants things Mother doesn't tell us,” said Roberta.

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: “That's right, Miss Goody-goody,” said Peter, “preach away.”

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: “I'M not goody,” said Phyllis, “but I think Bobbie's right this time.”

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: “Of course.

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: She always is.

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: In her own opinion,” said Peter.

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: “Oh, DON'T!” cried Roberta, putting down her egg-spoon; “don't let's be horrid to each other.

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: I'm sure some dire calamity is happening.

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: Don't let's make it worse!”

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: “Who began, I should like to know?” said Peter.

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: Roberta made an effort, and answered:--

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: “I did, I suppose, but--”

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: “Well, then,” said Peter, triumphantly.

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: But before he went to school he thumped his sister between the shoulders and told her to cheer up.

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: The children came home to one o'clock dinner, but Mother was not there.

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: And she was not there at tea-time.

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: It was nearly seven before she came in, looking so ill and tired that the children felt they could not ask her any questions.

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: She sank into an arm-chair.

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: Phyllis took the long pins out of her hat, while Roberta took off her gloves, and Peter unfastened her walking-shoes and fetched her soft velvety slippers for her.

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: When she had had a cup of tea, and Roberta had put eau-de-Cologne on her poor head that ached, Mother said:--

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: “Now, my darlings, I want to tell you something.

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: Those men last night did bring very bad news, and Father will be away for some time.

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: I am very worried about it, and I want you all to help me, and not to make things harder for me.”

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: “As if we would!” said Roberta, holding Mother's hand against her face.

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: “You can help me very much,” said Mother, “by being good and happy and not quarrelling when I'm away”--Roberta and Peter exchanged guilty glances--“for I shall have to be away a good deal.”

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: “We won't quarrel.

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: Indeed we won't,” said everybody.

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: And meant it, too.

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: “Then,” Mother went on, “I want you not to ask me any questions about this trouble; and not to ask anybody else any questions.”

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: Peter cringed and shuffled his boots on the carpet.

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: “You'll promise this, too, won't you?” said Mother.

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: “I did ask Ruth,” said Peter, suddenly. “I'm very sorry, but I did.”

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: “And what did she say?”

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: “She said I should know soon enough.”

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: “It isn't necessary for you to know anything about it,” said Mother; “it's about business, and you never do understand business, do you?”

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: “No,” said Roberta; “is it something to do with Government?

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: For Father was in a Government Office.

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: “Yes,” said Mother. “Now it's bed-time, my darlings.

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: And don't YOU worry.

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: It'll all come right in the end.”

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: “Then don't YOU worry either, Mother,” said Phyllis, “and we'll all be as good as gold.”

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: Mother sighed and kissed them.

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: “We'll begin being good the first thing tomorrow morning,” said Peter, as they went upstairs.

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: “Why not NOW?” said Roberta.

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: “There's nothing to be good ABOUT now, silly,” said Peter.

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: “We might begin to try to FEEL good,” said Phyllis, “and not call names.”

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: “Who's calling names?” said Peter. “Bobbie knows right enough that when I say 'silly', it's just the same as if I said Bobbie.”

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: “WELL,” said Roberta.

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: “No, I don't mean what you mean.

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: I mean it's just a--what is it Father calls it?--a germ of endearment!

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: Good night.”

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: The girls folded up their clothes with more than usual neatness--which was the only way of being good that they could think of.

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: “I say,” said Phyllis, smoothing out her pinafore, “you used to say it was so dull--nothing happening, like in books.

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: Now something HAS happened.”

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: “I never wanted things to happen to make Mother unhappy,” said Roberta. “Everything's perfectly horrid.”

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: Everything continued to be perfectly horrid for some weeks.

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: Mother was nearly always out.

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: Meals were dull and dirty.

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: The between-maid was sent away, and Aunt Emma came on a visit.

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: Aunt Emma was much older than Mother.

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: She was going abroad to be a governess.

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: She was very busy getting her clothes ready, and they were very ugly, dingy clothes, and she had them always littering about, and the sewing-machine seemed to whir--on and on all day and most of the night.

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: Aunt Emma believed in keeping children in their proper places.

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: And they more than returned the compliment.

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: Their idea of Aunt Emma's proper place was anywhere where they were not.

sentences.section: The Railway Children
sentences.sourceSentence: So they saw very little of her.
